title: The unripe word
hookLine: without the True Guru, other words are unripe (Anand 24)

lines: A MANGO AT A FRUIT STALL.
A MARKET WORD IN THE ANAND.
cards: A fruit stall in Amritsar. A woman picks up a mango, presses it with her thumb, and puts it back. Kacha, she says.
Unripe. She tries another that gives a little and smells sweet. Pakka.
Ripe. Those two words run all through Punjabi and Hindi. A kacha road is dirt; a pakka road is paved.
A kacha house is mud; a pakka house is brick. Kacha means not ready yet: not fired, not finished. Guru Amar Das took that market word and set it into the Anand.

teach.b: Pauri twenty-three calls out to the Sikhs of the True Guru: come and sing the true bani, the true word. Pauri twenty-four turns the coin over.

teach.h: PAURI 24: WITHOUT THE GURU, WORDS ARE RAW.
teach.b: Its refrain says, in paraphrase, that without the True Guru every other word is kachee, unripe. Then the circle widens.
Those who say such words are unripe. Those who hear them are unripe. Those who explain them are unripe.

teach.h: RIPE: A TRUE SOURCE, A PRESENT MIND.
teach.b: Even someone who repeats the Lord's name all day may not understand a thing, if the mind has been carried off by maya, the pull of the passing world.
So the problem isn't vocabulary; holy words can be said in an unripe way. The pauri points at two things: where a word comes from, and the mind that receives it.
For Sikhs, the ripe word is gurbani, the Gurus' own words, gathered in the Guru Granth Sahib.
The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks that the kirtan sung in the congregation be gurbani, along with the writings of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. There's an everyday edge, too.
Plenty of what gets said in a day is a little kacha: the half-heard rumor, the quick hot take, the reply typed before the message was finished. The pauri doesn't ask anyone to go silent.
It asks whether a word has a true source, and whether it's ready.

how: Many Sikhs recite the full Anand Sahib in the morning, and pauri 24's warning about unripe words is often cited to explain why kirtan in the gurdwara is drawn from gurbani.

o: a short prayer said in a hurry
unripe, raw, not from the True Guru
a word spoken in the Punjabi tongue

games.q: ripe and unripe — tap the pairs.
p: without the True Guru, words are unripe

s: pauri 24 says only the speakers of unripe words are unripe
it names the speakers, the hearers and the explainers too.
the pauri says holy words can still be said in an unripe way
a tongue can repeat the Name while the mind is carried off by maya.
the Rehat Maryada asks that congregational kirtan come from gurbani and a few named writers
gurbani, with the writings of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal.

games.q: a message makes you angry and your reply is already typed. by the logic of pauri 24, what would make it ripe?
o: using the right holy words in it.
its source, and a mind that is actually present.
sending it fast, before the moment passes.
games.why: the pauri says even the Lord's name can be said unripely; ripeness depends on where a word comes from and the mind behind it.

practice: Let one sentence from the last day come up that was a little kacha: said too fast, half true, or said to win.

Don't argue with it; just notice it, the way the woman at the stall feels the mango and sets it down, then rest with the breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, quietly, and let the rest be silence.

wordCard.voice: Kachee, unripe or raw. Kachee baanee: in the Anand, any word that doesn't come from the True Guru, or is said by a mind somewhere else. This week: bliss known through the Guru, given not grabbed, the narrow way, treasure within, and now ripe words.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kachee, unripe or raw; pauri 24's refrain calls every word without the True Guru kachee.

carryVoice: Your line: ripe words. Some words need one more breath before they're ready. That's day three hundred ninety-two.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on kirtan in the congregation
